Business Rules Engine - HLD

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate–Advanced Prerequisites: Message Queues, Caching Asked at: Amazon, Flipkart, Razorpay, PayPal, Uber, Goldman Sachs

TL;DR

A business rules engine decouples decision logic from application code. Product teams author rules (“if order > $500 AND user is new, apply 10% discount”) via a management UI. The engine evaluates incoming events against thousands of active rules in sub-50ms, then triggers actions without redeploying any service.

In 3 sentences: Rule authors define conditions as structured expressions (stored as pre-parsed abstract syntax trees, or ASTs, in JSONB). The evaluation engine loads compiled rules from in-memory cache, runs them through a Rete network for shared sub-expression optimization, and collects matches in < 50ms. Matched actions are dispatched via Kafka to a decoupled executor with retries and dead-letter queues (DLQs).💡 An abstract syntax tree (AST) is the condition stored as a tree of nodes instead of as text: total > 500 AND tier == 'NEW' becomes an AND node with two comparison children. Trees can be walked and checked; strings have to be re-parsed every time, which is the whole point of doing it once at write time.

Functional Requirements

Core (top 3)

  1. Author and manage rules — CRUD rules with structured conditions (comparisons, arithmetic, boolean logic, nested expressions), assign actions, activate/deactivate, version with rollback.
  2. Evaluate events against rules — given an event payload (JSON), find all matching rules and return decisions + trigger actions, in < 50ms P99 (the latency 99% of requests beat) for 10K active rules.💡 P99 is the slow tail rather than the average: 99 of every 100 evaluations must finish under 50ms. Designing against the tail matters because this engine sits inside someone else’s checkout request.
  3. Hot reload without downtime — when a rule changes, all engine instances pick up the new version within 2 seconds without restart or dropped evaluations.

Below the line

  • Visual rule builder UI (assume it calls our API).
  • A/B testing of rule variants.
  • Rule simulation across historical event datasets.
  • Multi-tenant isolation at the compute level (we do namespace isolation only).
  • Complex event processing (time-windowed correlations across multiple events).

Non-Functional Requirements

  • Latency — P99 evaluation < 50ms for 10K active rules against a single event.
  • Throughput — 50K evaluations/sec per engine instance, horizontally scalable.
  • Consistency — rule changes propagated to all instances within 2s. Strong consistency for blocking rules via direct DB read.
  • Auditability — full immutable execution log for compliance.

Core Entities

  • Rule — named decision unit: identity, namespace, priority, status (DRAFT/ACTIVE/DISABLED/ARCHIVED), pointer to current version.
  • Rule Version — immutable snapshot of condition AST + actions. Full history for rollback.
  • Condition (AST Node) — tree node representing one logic piece. Recursively composed.
  • Action — what fires on match: webhook, email, field enrichment, block/allow, DB update.
  • Event — incoming payload to evaluate: JSON with type and arbitrary fields.
  • Namespace — logical rule grouping (e.g., fraud-detection, pricing). Evaluated together.
  • Execution Record — audit trail: event ID, matched rules, actions, latency.

API / System Interface

POST   /v1/rules                          -> Rule
GET    /v1/rules/:id                      -> Rule + current version
PUT    /v1/rules/:id                      -> new version created
DELETE /v1/rules/:id                      -> soft delete (ARCHIVED)
POST   /v1/rules/:id/activate             -> set status ACTIVE
POST   /v1/rules/:id/deactivate           -> set status DISABLED
POST   /v1/rules/:id/rollback/:version    -> revert to prior version
GET    /v1/rules/:id/versions             -> paginated version history
POST   /v1/evaluate                       -> EvaluationResult
POST   /v1/evaluate/dry-run               -> EvaluationResult (no actions fired)
GET    /v1/executions?event_id=X          -> execution audit records
BASH

Example — create a rule:

POST /v1/rules
{
  "namespace": "fraud-detection",
  "name": "high-value-new-user-block",
  "condition": "order.total > 500 AND user.tier == 'NEW' AND user.country IN ['NG','GH']",
  "actions": [
    { "type": "BLOCK_TRANSACTION", "reason": "High value new user from high-risk region" },
    { "type": "WEBHOOK", "url": "https://fraud-team.internal/review" }
  ],
  "priority": 100
}
JSON

The API parses the condition string into an AST at write time (ANTLR), validates it, stores the AST in rule_versions.condition_ast.💡 ANTLR is a parser generator: you describe the condition language’s grammar once and it produces the code that turns a condition string into a tree. Using a generator rather than hand-written string-splitting is what gives authors precise “unexpected token at position 15” errors.

Example — evaluate:

POST /v1/evaluate
{
  "namespace": "fraud-detection",
  "event_type": "order.created",
  "event_id": "evt_abc123",
  "payload": {
    "order": { "total": 750, "currency": "USD" },
    "user": { "id": "u_99", "tier": "NEW", "country": "NG" }
  }
}
// Response: { "evaluation_time_ms": 12.4, "matched_rules": [...], "final_decision": "BLOCK" }
JSON

Security notes:

  • JSON Web Token (JWT) auth on all endpoints; namespace-scoped permissions.💡 A JWT is a signed blob the client presents with each request; because the server signed it, the server can trust the user id inside without a database lookup. Here it is what lets us scope an author to the namespaces they own.
  • dry-run evaluates but never fires actions — for testing rules pre-activation.
  • Event payloads encrypted at rest; personally identifiable information (PII) masked in audit logs by default.

High-Level Design

FR-1: Author and Manage Rules

New components:

A rule is a condition and an action. Authors write the condition as a string, because that is what a human can read and review, and we store it.

New components:

  1. Rules API — HTTP service for CRUD, versioning and the draft/active lifecycle.
  2. Postgres (rules + rule_versions) — durable store. Every edit creates a new immutable version.

Step-by-step:

  1. Author submits a rule with a condition string, e.g. order.total > 500 AND user.tier == 'NEW', plus the action to take
  2. Rules API stores it as a new rule_versions row with the condition kept verbatim as text
  3. Status starts DRAFT. The author calls POST /activate when ready, which flips it to ACTIVE
  4. The API returns the version number

Why version on every edit: Compliance requires knowing which logic was active at any point. Immutable versions make rollback trivial — just repoint current_version — and they mean an audit record can name the exact rule text that fired.

Why a draft state at all? Because a rule is production logic written by someone who is often not an engineer, and activating it is a deploy. Separating “saved” from “live” is what makes review possible.

What we have deliberately left broken. Rules can be authored, versioned and activated, and the audit trail is sound. One thing step 2 does not do:

It stores the condition without ever checking that it means anything. A typo, an unknown field, an unbalanced parenthesis — all accepted, all ACTIVE, and all discovered at evaluation time in production rather than at the moment someone typed them. The author gets a 200; the on-call engineer gets the error. That is Deep Dive 3.

FR-2: Evaluate Events Against Rules

New components:

An event arrives and we need to know which rules match it, then do what those rules say.

New components:

  1. Evaluation Engine — the hot path. Holds the active rule set in memory and checks an incoming event against it.
  2. In-Memory Rule Cache — each engine loads the full active rule set at startup, so evaluation never makes a network call to fetch a rule.

Step-by-step:

  1. Calling service sends POST /evaluate with the event payload
  2. Engine takes the rule set from local memory — no network hop
  3. It loops over every rule, evaluates that rule’s condition against the event, and collects the matches
  4. For each match, in priority order, it performs the action: send the email, call the webhook, apply the discount
  5. It writes an audit record naming which rule version fired
  6. It returns the result to the caller

Why hold rules in memory rather than fetching them per evaluation? Because evaluation touches the whole rule set, not one rule. At 10K rules and 0.5ms per Redis round trip, fetching them individually is 5 seconds for a single evaluation against a 50ms P99 budget. The rule set has to be in-process; that is not negotiable and not a deep dive.💡 In-process means the data lives in the same program’s own memory, so reading it costs nanoseconds and no network is involved. A cache in Redis is still a network hop away, and 10,000 hops will never fit in 50ms.

What we have deliberately left broken. Events get evaluated and actions get taken, with an audit trail. Two properties of this loop fail, for unrelated reasons:

  • Step 3 is a linear scan that re-evaluates shared work. Every rule is checked independently, so if 400 rules all begin order.total > 500, that comparison runs 400 times per event. The cost is O(rules) per event with a large constant, against a 50ms P99. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Step 4 performs actions inline, inside the caller’s request. So the caller’s latency includes an external email API, and — worse — a failure halfway through a rule’s actions leaves some done and some not, with no retry and no record of which. The caller gets a 500 for an evaluation that was actually correct. That is Deep Dive 4.

FR-3: Hot Reload Without Downtime

New components:

FR-2 loads the rule set once at startup, which means a rule activated now does nothing until someone restarts the fleet. Restarting production to change a discount threshold is not a workflow anyone will accept, so the engines have to pick up changes while running.

New components:

  1. Cache Refresh Loop — a background thread in each engine that re-reads the active rule set from Postgres on a timer and replaces its in-memory copy.

Step-by-step:

  1. The author activates version 7. The Rules API writes it to Postgres and returns
  2. Every engine runs a loop that wakes every 30 seconds and queries the active rule set for its namespace
  3. It compares the versions it got against the ones it holds
  4. If anything changed, it builds the new rule set and replaces its in-memory reference
  5. In-flight evaluations finish against the old set; subsequent ones use the new one

Why replace the whole set rather than patch the changed rule? Because a partially-updated rule set is a state nobody designed. Rules interact through priority ordering, so applying one change in isolation can produce an ordering that no version of the rule set ever had. Swapping the whole thing means the engine is always running some coherent published version.

What we have deliberately left broken. Rules now take effect without a deploy, which is what the requirement asked. The polling is crude in three specific ways:

  • Up to 30 seconds of lag, and for a rule written to stop a live incident — blocking a fraudulent merchant, disabling a broken promotion — 30 seconds is the whole point of the rule.
  • Engines disagree with each other during the window. This is the one that matters most and is easiest to miss: instance A may have polled and instance B not yet, so the same event sent twice gets two different answers depending on which instance answers. The system is briefly non-deterministic, and the audit log will record both.
  • Every engine queries Postgres every 30 seconds forever, almost always to be told nothing changed. The load scales with fleet size and has nothing to do with how often rules actually change.

All three are Deep Dive 2.

Technology Choices

Tier / Purpose What it stores Primary pick Alternatives
Rule definitions rules, versions, AST as JSONB PostgreSQL MySQL, CockroachDB
Execution audit which rules fired per event PostgreSQL partitioned by day Cassandra, ClickHouse
In-memory cache compiled Rete network per namespace Local process memory Hazelcast
L2 cache serialized rule set per namespace Redis Memcached
Change propagation rule.updated events Kafka Redis Pub/Sub, NATS
Action dispatch matched actions to execute Kafka SQS, RabbitMQ
Expression parsing tokenize conditions at write time ANTLR Custom recursive descent
Dead letter queue failed actions after max retries Kafka DLQ topic SQS DLQ
scroll →

Why pre-parsed AST in Postgres, not raw expression strings?

Parsing at evaluation time is expensive and error-prone. By parsing at write time and storing the AST as JSONB, the engine never touches a parser on the hot path. It loads a tree, walks it. Authors get syntax errors immediately, not when a customer triggers the rule.💡 JSONB is Postgres’s binary JSON column type - it stores the parsed structure rather than the raw text, so the database can index and query inside the tree. Here it means the condition tree is a first-class column instead of an opaque string.

Why local in-memory cache, not just Redis?

Redis ~0.5ms per GET. With 10K rules and a Rete network, reconstructing from serialized data per request is too slow. Each engine holds the full compiled network in memory. Redis is L2 for cold starts and consistency signals.💡 L2 means the second-level cache: the engine’s own memory is L1 and is checked first, and Redis is only consulted when L1 is empty - typically a freshly started process. The alternative to an L2 is every cold engine hammering Postgres at once.

Data Modeling

Postgres Schemas

CREATE TABLE rules (
    rule_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    namespace VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    priority INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    status VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'DRAFT',
    current_version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_by VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_rules_ns ON rules(namespace, status);

CREATE TABLE rule_versions (
    version_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    rule_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES rules(rule_id),
    version_number INTEGER NOT NULL,
    condition_ast JSONB NOT NULL,  -- pre-parsed AST
    actions JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_by VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE(rule_id, version_number)
);

CREATE TABLE rule_executions (
    execution_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_id VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    namespace VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    rules_evaluated INTEGER NOT NULL,
    rules_matched INTEGER NOT NULL,
    evaluation_time_ms REAL NOT NULL,
    matched_rule_ids UUID[],
    actions_triggered JSONB NOT NULL,
    evaluated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    -- Postgres requires every unique/primary key on a partitioned table to
    -- include the partition key, so evaluated_at is part of the PK.
    PRIMARY KEY (execution_id, evaluated_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (evaluated_at);
SQL

AST JSON Structure (stored in condition_ast JSONB)

{
  "type": "AND",
  "children": [
    {
      "type": "COMPARISON", "operator": ">",
      "left": { "type": "FIELD_REF", "path": "order.total_amount" },
      "right": { "type": "LITERAL", "value": 500, "dataType": "NUMBER" }
    },
    {
      "type": "COMPARISON", "operator": "==",
      "left": { "type": "FIELD_REF", "path": "user.tier" },
      "right": { "type": "LITERAL", "value": "NEW", "dataType": "STRING" }
    }
  ]
}
JSON

Supported node types: COMPARISON (>, <, >=, <=, ==, !=, IN, CONTAINS), ARITHMETIC (+, -, *, /), BOOLEAN (AND, OR, NOT), FIELD_REF (dot-path into event payload), LITERAL (typed constant), FUNCTION (built-ins like NOW(), LENGTH(), UPPER()).

Redis Cache Patterns

"rules:compiled:{namespace}" → Serialized rule set (protobuf). No TTL, invalidated via Kafka.
"rules:version:{namespace}" → Integer version counter. Used for cache-busting.
"rules:lock:{namespace}"    → Distributed lock during reload (TTL: 5s).

Deep Dives

1) 400 rules all start with the same comparison. Why do we run it 400 times?

Evaluate an event against 10K rules in < 50ms.

Bad — the linear loop FR-2 built: Iterate every rule, evaluate condition tree. O(N) with N=10K rules × 5 conditions = 50K checks. ~200ms. Fails P99 budget.💡 O(N) is shorthand for “the work grows in direct proportion to the number of rules” - double the rules and you double the time. That is the property we need to break, because the rule count is set by product teams and only ever goes up.

Iterate every rule, evaluate condition tree. O(N) with N=10K rules × 5 conditions = 50K checks. ~200ms. Fails P99 budget.

Pre-compile each AST into a function. Evaluate in parallel (thread pool), short-circuit AND/OR early. Gets to ~30ms with 8 threads. Problem: many rules share sub-conditions (e.g., 200 rules all check ). Same condition evaluated 200 times.

Build a discrimination network at compile time:

Event fields asserted once into the network. Shared conditions evaluated once, result propagates to all dependents. For 10K rules with 60% overlap, effective evaluations drop from 50K to ~8K. P99: 12-20ms.

Trade-off: Rete networks use more memory (~50MB per namespace for 10K rules). Acceptable for in-memory engines.

2) Two engines hold different rule sets for 30 seconds. How do we push a change instead?

How to update rules across a fleet without restart or stale evaluations.

Worth dismissing first: requiring a restart, which is where FR-2 left us before FR-3 existed. Deploying rules as config and rolling-restarting the fleet takes 5-10 minutes for 50 pods, and the whole rollout window has some pods on old rules and some on new. For a fraud rule that window is money.

Bad — the 30-second poll FR-3 built. It clears the restart bar and has three defects, and the lag is the least interesting of them.

The lag is real: up to 30 seconds before a rule takes effect, and a rule written to stop a live incident is the case where that matters most.

The divergence is worse. Each engine polls on its own schedule, so for up to 30 seconds instance A holds version 7 and instance B holds version 6. The same event, sent twice, gets two different answers depending on which instance picks it up — and both land in the audit log as authoritative. A rules engine that is non-deterministic for 30 seconds after every change is hard to reason about and harder to explain to an auditor.

And the cost is constant and misdirected: every engine queries Postgres every 30 seconds forever, almost always to learn that nothing changed. Load scales with fleet size rather than with how often rules change, which is backwards.

A rules engine that is non-deterministic for 30 seconds after every change is hard to reason about and harder to explain to an auditor.

And the : every engine queries Postgres every 30 seconds forever, almost always to learn that nothing changed. Load scales with fleet size rather than with how often rules change, which is backwards.

Have the Rules API publish to Redis Pub/Sub on activation; engines subscribe and rebuild on the message. Propagation drops from 30 seconds to milliseconds and the idle polling disappears. The gap is delivery: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget, so an engine that was restarting or briefly partitioned never receives the message and stays stale indefinitely — until the change happens to wake it. That converts a bounded 30-second staleness into an unbounded one, which is arguably worse than what we started with.

Publish to Kafka so an engine that was down catches up from its offset on restart, and have each engine compare versions rather than trusting that it saw every message. Then add:

3) A typo in a condition reaches production. Where should a rule be rejected?

Turn order.total > 500 AND user.tier == 'NEW' into a validated, executable AST.

Bad — interpreting the raw condition string at evaluation time, which is all FR-1 left us: it stored the text without validating it, so the first thing that ever parses a rule is the hot path, in production, on a real event. Done with a language-level eval() it is also a remote code execution hole — the condition is attacker-adjacent text being handed to an interpreter: Store condition as raw string, eval() at evaluation time. Security nightmare (injection), terrible performance (re-parse every call), impossible to validate field references statically.💡 eval() hands a string to the language’s own interpreter and runs it as program code. Anyone who can save a rule can therefore run code on our servers, which is why the condition language is parsed by a grammar we control instead.

which is all FR-1 left us: it stored the text without validating it, so the first thing that ever parses a rule is the hot path, in production, on a real event. Done with a language-level it is also a remote code execution hole — the condition is attacker-adjacent text being handed to an interpreter: Store condition as raw string, at evaluation time. Security nightmare (injection), terrible performance (re-parse every call), impossible to validate field references statically.

Hand-rolled tokenizer → recursive descent → AST. Works, but inconsistent operator precedence, poor error messages, and every new operator requires manual parser changes.

Define a formal grammar in ANTLR (expression → comparison | boolean combinator | parenthesized sub-expression). ANTLR generates lexer + parser. A custom Visitor walks the parse tree and builds our AST JSON structure. Benefits:

Parsing runs once at write time (~2ms per rule). Stored AST loaded at evaluation time with zero parsing overhead.

4) Two of a rule’s three actions fired, then the email API timed out. What now?

When a rule matches, trigger actions reliably without blocking evaluation.

Bad — the inline execution FR-2 step 4 built, which puts every external call inside the caller’s request and leaves a half-applied rule with no record of how far it got: Fire webhook synchronously before returning response. Webhook timeout (3s) destroys evaluation P99. Action failure shouldn’t block the evaluation.

which puts every external call inside the caller’s request and leaves a half-applied rule with no record of how far it got: Fire webhook synchronously before returning response. Webhook timeout (3s) destroys evaluation P99. Action failure shouldn’t block the evaluation.

Publish to Kafka, return immediately. If action fails, it’s lost. For fraud alerts that’s unacceptable.

Core Flows

Flow 1: Create and Activate a Rule

Walkthrough:

  1. Author submits a rule with a human-readable condition. API parses via ANTLR, validates, stores as DRAFT.
  2. Author tests via POST /evaluate/dry-run to confirm behavior.
  3. Author activates. API updates Postgres, publishes to Kafka, pre-populates Redis.
  4. Engine instances consume the event, fetch from Redis, rebuild Rete network, swap atomically.
  5. Next evaluation uses the new rule. Total time from activation to live: < 2 seconds.

Failure path: If Kafka is unavailable when API publishes the change event, the rule is active in Postgres but engines don’t know. Safety net: engines do a periodic full-sync every 60s (poll Postgres namespace version), bounding staleness even if Kafka has an outage.

Flow 2: Evaluate an Event

Walkthrough:

  1. Calling service sends event. Engine loads Rete network from local memory.
  2. Event fields asserted into alpha nodes. Shared conditions evaluated once.
  3. Matched rules collected, priority-sorted. Synchronous response in ~12ms.
  4. Async: actions published to Kafka, audit record written to Postgres.
  5. Action Executor delivers webhooks with retry logic.

Failure path: Engine crashes after returning evaluation but before publishing actions to Kafka. Caller got BLOCK (correct), but fraud team webhook never fires. Mitigation: write an outbox record to Postgres alongside the audit log. Outbox poller picks up un-published actions and retries.

Interview Tips

  1. Lead with the AST insight. “I’d store rules as pre-parsed ASTs, not raw strings. Parsing at write time, evaluation is just tree traversal.” Shows hot-path vs cold-path split understanding.

  2. Name Rete. Most candidates loop linearly. Mention shared sub-condition optimization. Amazon and Goldman specifically look for this.

  3. Draw the Kafka boundary early. Evaluation is synchronous and fast; action execution is async and reliable. Shows decoupling principle.

  4. Hot reload is the trap question. Have the Kafka + atomic swap + version check story ready.

  5. Dry-run is your testing story. Prevents bad rules from breaking production. Version history + instant rollback + AST validation at write time.

  6. Compliance at financial companies. At Goldman, PayPal, Razorpay: immutable audit trail. Every evaluation logged. Every version preserved. Answer “what rule was active at 3:47 PM March 12?” from rule_versions.

  7. Anchor with scale numbers. 10K active rules, 50K evals/sec, < 50ms P99. Realistic for a payment fraud engine.
